work.heading: How the nineteenth century remade Christmas.
work.note: The history begins with customs already fading before 1837 — kissing boughs, Twelfth Night, wassailing — and follows the festival’s reshaping through cheaper postage, railways, mass publishing and consumer culture.

editorial.heading: One chronology for objects, labour and literature.
editorial.note: Trees, cards and crackers are treated as developments with histories rather than timeless props, so a single custom can be followed on its own or read across the whole period.

reading.heading: Invention, labour and the printed festival.
reading.note: Three routes through the history: which traditions are younger than they appear, whose work sustained the family celebration, and how cards, carols and ghost stories made Christmas a shared image.

work.heading: From Gateshead to the terms of her own life.
work.note: The account below follows Jane through Gateshead, Lowood, Thornfield and Moor House, and the question of how much of herself she should surrender for love, duty, respectability or safety.

editorial.heading: Brontë’s text, with the commentary kept out of its way.
editorial.note: Spelling and punctuation stand as Brontë left them, context appears in boxes after each chapter, and the essays run from the Bell pseudonyms to the afterlives of Jane, Rochester and Bertha Mason.

reading.heading: Independence, four houses and a narrating voice.
reading.note: Three routes follow Jane’s refusals of dependence, the houses that test her belonging, and the adult narrator who insists on the right to interpret her own life.

work.heading: Redlaw’s bargain and the last of the Christmas books.
work.note: The account below follows the phantom’s gift from Redlaw to the people around him, and ends where the book’s stage history does, with the scene that became Pepper’s Ghost.

editorial.heading: A light hand with the 1848 text.
editorial.note: Dickens’s spelling, capitalisation and paragraphing stand, with the regularisations stated; the notes stay outside the story, from Victorian chemistry to ragged schools.

reading.heading: Memory, experiment and a ghost on stage.
reading.note: The routes below ask what sympathy owes to painful memory, what happens when feeling becomes an experiment, and how one scene passed into Victorian optical entertainment.

work.heading: One June day in post-war London.
work.note: The account below follows Clarissa and Septimus through the city, and the clocks, crowds and party that join their separate stories.

editorial.heading: Twelve breaks restored, four declared additions.
editorial.note: The notes below say where the reading text comes from and which divisions are Woolf’s own rather than added Parts.

reading.heading: Clocks, doctors and the party.
reading.note: The routes below follow the striking hours that join two minds, the treatment of Septimus, and what Clarissa’s party attempts.

work.heading: The voyage, the crime and the compulsion to retell.
work.note: The account below follows the Mariner from the ice to Life-in-Death, and the storytelling that his punishment demands of him.

editorial.heading: The 1834 text, its gloss and its commentary.
editorial.note: Commentary sits at the foot of the page, while the introduction traces the poem from Lyrical Ballads through decades of revision.

reading.heading: An unexplained shooting, a double voice, an endless tale.
reading.note: Three routes into the poem: guilt without motive, the gloss that does not quite agree with the verse, and narration as penance.

work.heading: Werther’s letters and the life behind them.
work.note: The account below follows the novel’s story, the limits of its letters and the events of 1772 that Goethe drew into fiction.

editorial.heading: Eighty-eight letters, thirty chapters, two versions.
editorial.note: The dated letters keep their sequence within thirty editorial chapters, and the essays range from Ossian and Sturm und Drang to the disputed Werther effect.

reading.heading: Perspective, biography and a European sensation.
reading.note: Three routes into the novel: what the letters cannot show, how lived events became fiction, and the imitation and censorship that followed publication.

work.heading: Twenty-eight years on the island.
work.note: The account below follows Crusoe from York and Brazil to the 1659 shipwreck, the footprint and the rescue of Friday.

editorial.heading: A modernised text that keeps the journal’s dates.
editorial.note: Defoe’s long sentences survive, the twenty chapters are declared editorial, and the notes run from Alexander Selkirk to later adaptation.

reading.heading: Work, Providence and empire.
reading.note: Three routes follow Crusoe’s conversion of survival into property, the rival explanations of his deliverance, and the authority he claims over Friday.

work.heading: Fourteen works from the early Tudor court.
work.note: The account below sets out the selection, from formal elegy to Skeltonic satire, and names the longer poems given as declared extracts.

editorial.heading: Old spelling kept, Dyce’s apparatus set aside.
editorial.note: Line numbers, glossary and footnotes make the 1843 text usable, with essays reaching from Wolsey’s court to the Skeltonic line.

reading.heading: Rhyme, court and the shape of a selection.
reading.note: The routes below follow the drive of the Skeltonic line, the dangers of writing close to power, and what this selection includes and cuts.

work.heading: Achilles’ anger in Butler’s prose.
work.note: The account below follows the poem from the quarrel with Agamemnon to the funeral of Hector, and shows how Butler’s 1898 prose and the notes open the poem to readers without ancient Greek.

editorial.heading: Homer, Butler and the Homeric question, book by book.
editorial.note: Summaries and context boxes accompany all twenty-four books, while the longer essays introduce Homer, Butler, oral tradition and the possible history behind Troy.

reading.heading: Anger, mortality and an ending in mourning.
reading.note: The routes below follow the cost of Achilles’ withdrawal, the worth of glory to people who die, and the meeting between Priam and Achilles that closes the poem without conquest.

work.heading: The 1609 sequence, complete.
work.note: The account below follows all 154 sonnets in the quarto order, from the opening marriage plea to the dark-haired woman and the closing Cupid myths.

editorial.heading: The quarto explained, each poem kept whole.
editorial.note: The introduction runs from Thorpe’s 1609 printing and the dedication to Mr W. H. to the English sonnet’s development, while every page holds one complete poem.

reading.heading: Sequence, time and unnamed addressees.
reading.note: Three routes follow how neighbouring sonnets alter one another, the claim that verse outlasts decay, and the biography the poems withhold.

work.heading: From Venus’s pursuit to the fall of the Roman kings.
work.note: The account below follows each poem’s story and what the pair reveal when read together, from erotic comedy to political change.

editorial.heading: A modernised text of the 1593 and 1594 quartos.
editorial.note: The text keeps Shakespeare’s wording, stanza forms and rhyme; the essays and glossary described below stand apart from the poems themselves.

reading.heading: Desire, testimony and a name made in print.
reading.note: Three routes through the pair: persuasion met by refusal, the burden of speaking about violence, and the quartos that established Shakespeare’s literary reputation.

work.heading: The Countess episode and the French campaigns.
work.note: The account below follows both movements of the play: Edward’s pursuit of the Countess of Salisbury, and the campaigns in France that test the Black Prince.

editorial.heading: A modernised quarto and the authorship question.
editorial.note: The 1596 text appears in modern spelling with scene summaries and foot-of-page notes, while the introductions weigh Shakespeare’s contribution and the unsettled identity of his collaborator.

reading.heading: Self-command, honour and a disputed canon.
reading.note: Three routes measure the king against his private desire, follow how the Black Prince earns honour, and trace the play’s changing place at the boundary of Shakespeare’s works.

work.heading: Alice Arden’s conspiracy and its failures.
work.note: The plot against Thomas Arden runs through detected poison, locked doors, misfiring weapons and fog before succeeding at home; the quarrel with Mosbie stands at the play’s psychological centre.

editorial.heading: A modernised quarto and the authorship question.
editorial.note: The 1592 first quarto is given in modernised spelling with scene summaries, line numbers and same-page notes, while the introduction weighs Holinshed, the three quartos and the competing claims for Shakespeare and Kyd.

reading.heading: The household, providence and attribution.
reading.note: Three routes into the tragedy: catastrophe relocated to an ordinary house, failures that read as comedy or judgement, and a quarrel scene that tests stylistic authorship study.

work.heading: Legendary Britain from Brutus to the Severn.
work.note: The account below follows the tragedy of Locrine, Gwendoline and Estrild alongside Strumbo’s comic career, with the five dumb shows in which Ate forecasts ruin.

editorial.heading: A modernised text and the case of W. S.
editorial.note: The 1595 quarto appears in modern spelling with line numbers and same-page notes, while the introduction weighs W. S., Charles Tilney, Greene and Peele against the later Shakespeare claim.

reading.heading: Origins, emblems and two initials.
reading.note: Three routes follow the broken settlement of legendary Britain, the play’s inherited Senecan forms, and the title-page initials that carried it into the Third Folio.

work.heading: From Ill May Day to the scaffold.
work.note: The account below follows More’s rise and fall and places the Hand D pages within the Ill May Day scene.

editorial.heading: The manuscript’s working state, kept visible.
editorial.note: Additions, damage and unfinished passages stand in the modernised text, with introductions on the six hands, Tilney’s censorship and the stage.

reading.heading: Strangers, conscience and six hands.
reading.note: The routes below follow the Ill May Day appeal, More’s refusal of the king’s articles, and the revising hands that shaped the document.

work.heading: From a blacksmith’s house to condemnation without trial.
work.note: The account below follows the play’s Cromwell through Europe and the court, and marks where the drama departs from the historical record.

editorial.heading: A modernised play and its disputed quartos.
editorial.note: Scene summaries and same-page notes support the text, while the introduction weighs the W. S. attribution and the printings of 1602 and 1613.

reading.heading: Fortune, gratitude and history reshaped.
reading.note: Three routes through the play: advancement under unstable fortune, repayment as the measure of character, and chronicle drama set against biography.

work.heading: A Prodigal Son in the London credit economy.
work.note: The account below follows Flowerdale’s frauds and Luce’s disguised loyalty, and shows how the 1605 play measures ruin in bonds, sureties and arrest.

editorial.heading: A modernised quarto with the notes on the page.
editorial.note: The 1605 text is modernised and line-numbered, and the introduction takes on what the quarto raises: the title-page attribution, the performance claim and the patient-wife tradition.

reading.heading: Credit, patience and a name on the title page.
reading.note: Three routes follow the borrowed money that sustains Flowerdale’s standing, the unequal patience demanded of Luce, and why the company claim is credited while the author claim is rejected.

work.heading: A widow’s vow and Pyeboard’s profitable frauds.
work.note: The account below follows the conspiracy from the overheard vow to the exposure at the church door, played out across named London streets and parishes.

editorial.heading: A modern-spelling text and the case for Middleton.
editorial.note: The 1607 quarto is given in modern spelling with line numbers, and the introduction sets the W. S. initials against the attribution to Middleton.

reading.heading: Fraud as theatre, London as stage, and a disputed canon.
reading.note: The routes below follow the conspirators’ command of an audience, the city geography that grounds the jokes, and the attribution history that carried the play from W. S. to Middleton.

work.heading: Ten scenes from the Calverley case.
work.note: The play strips Walter Calverley’s 1605 attack on his family to Husband, Wife, children, debt and inheritance; what follows covers both the action and the 1608 quarto that carries it.

editorial.heading: The 1608 quarto and the introductions around it.
editorial.note: Original spelling is preserved and evident errors corrected, with verse and prose kept distinct; the introductions run from the Calverley case and title-page attribution to Middleton’s claim and the missing companion plays.

reading.heading: Debt, compression and true crime.
reading.note: Three routes into the tragedy: ruin turned into violence against a family, the relentlessness of ten short scenes, and a play that transforms recent reportage.

work.heading: From the Ghost’s command to the poisoned match.
work.note: The account below follows the play from the Ghost’s accusation to the fencing match Claudius prepares, as private grief becomes a crisis of evidence, surveillance, performance and succession.

editorial.heading: A conflated text built openly from Quarto and Folio.
editorial.note: The edition principally follows the Second Quarto while incorporating important Folio material, and its essays reach from ghosts and Purgatory to Ophelia, criticism, theatre and cinema.

reading.heading: Evidence, versions and four centuries on stage.
reading.note: Three routes ask how knowledge relates to action, what the three early texts preserve, and how theatres and films keep making fresh choices about motive, age, politics and ending.

work.heading: Two family tragedies and two early texts.
work.note: The account below follows Lear’s division of Britain and Gloucester’s deception into storm and civil war, and explains how the 1608 Quarto and 1623 Folio differ.

editorial.heading: A conflated Lear that shows its seams.
editorial.note: Quarto-only and Folio-only passages are signalled within the modern-spelling text, and forty key passages sit inside essays that run from a divided Britain to revision, madness and performance.

reading.heading: Authority, two texts and the problem of sight.
reading.note: Three routes ask what a king retains after giving his kingdom away, how possible revision changes the play’s shape, and why blindness and recognition yield no simple providential order.

work.heading: The lovers, the wood and the play within the play.
work.note: Hermia’s forced choice, Puck’s misapplied flower and the mechanicals’ Pyramus and Thisbe are followed here alongside the quarto and Folio evidence the text records.

editorial.heading: A modern-spelling text beside essays from folklore to ballet.
editorial.note: The play keeps its footnotes and line numbers on the page; the essays range from Athens and the English wood to fairies, marriage law, music, criticism, theatre, film and ballet.

reading.heading: Desire, the changeling quarrel and the watching of plays.
reading.note: Three routes through the comedy: how law and magic try to organise attachment, what Oberon and Titania’s dispute disturbs, and what Pyramus and Thisbe asks of its audience.

work.heading: From the Venetian Senate to a bedroom in Cyprus.
work.note: The account below follows the marriage, the move to Cyprus and Iago’s campaign of manufactured evidence.

editorial.heading: Same-page commentary and an extended introduction.
editorial.note: Scene summaries and notes sit beside the line-numbered text, while the introduction reaches from Quarto and Folio to race, double time and the stage.

reading.heading: Evidence, prejudice and two printed texts.
reading.note: The routes below follow Iago’s manufactured proof, Othello’s standing in Venice, and what the choice between Quarto and Folio changes in performance.

work.heading: From the witches’ greeting to Birnam Wood.
work.note: The account below follows the murder of Duncan into its consequences, and how equivocation works because a listener chooses the interpretation that protects desire.

editorial.heading: The Folio text with the Middleton question in view.
editorial.note: The only authoritative early text appears in modern spelling with same-page commentary, and forty key passages join essays reaching from Holinshed and James I to criticism, theatre and film.

reading.heading: Prophecy, marriage and an equivocal text.
reading.note: Three routes ask how prediction becomes tragedy, how the Macbeths’ shared purpose divides under guilt and secrecy, and what the Folio’s disputed material means for the play.

work.heading: Eight stories, four poems and the documents beside them.
work.note: The account below names the complete contents, from The Old Nurse’s Story to The Judge’s House, and the historical material that surrounds them.

editorial.heading: Complete texts, with fiction and document kept apart.
editorial.note: Notes accompany unabridged stories and poems, and the documents on séances and psychical research stay distinct from the fiction beside them.

reading.heading: Haunted places, disputed testimony, a changing tradition.
reading.note: Three routes through the collection: familiar spaces made dangerous, perception under question, and a form followed across half a century of publishing.

work.heading: Two stories from one magazine, 1891–92.
work.note: The account below restores their shared periodical setting and the medical, legal and domestic world in which Gilman wrote.

editorial.heading: Notes, variants and claims tested against evidence.
editorial.note: Footnotes handle period language, while textual history is kept separate from the anecdotes that have gathered around The Yellow Wallpaper.

reading.heading: The household, the magazine and the changing text.
reading.note: Three routes through the stories: authority at home, publication in The New England Magazine, and what repetition did to the record afterwards.

work.heading: Behn’s narrative of 1688.
work.note: The account below follows Oroonoko from betrayal at sea to the plantation rising in Surinam and its violent end.

editorial.heading: A modernised text with its evidence on show.
editorial.note: Notes, chronology and named sources support the reading text, while the essays weigh the disputed record of Behn’s Surinam years.

reading.heading: Broken promises, contested witness, two coasts.
reading.note: Three routes run from the freedoms offered and withdrawn to the story’s claim of eyewitness truth and the geography of Atlantic slavery.

work.heading: Fifteen poems from the Cuala Press.
work.note: The account below follows the collection from its 1920 printing to publication in 1921, and records the readings Yeats later altered.

editorial.heading: The Cuala wording, kept and annotated.
editorial.note: Line numbers and notes surround an unmodernised text, with supporting material running from the Easter Rising to Yeats’s marriage and automatic writing.

reading.heading: First readings, revolution and private systems.
reading.note: Three routes follow the poems as first printed, the politics of the Easter Rising, and the symbolic thought that grew into A Vision.

work.heading: The poems of 1798 and 1800 in their first forms.
work.note: The account below sets out the selection from both early editions, from the Ancyent Marinere and Tintern Abbey to the Lucy poems and Michael, each printed as it first entered Lyrical Ballads.

editorial.heading: Early printings kept, later revisions set aside.
editorial.note: Each poem keeps the spelling, punctuation and capitalisation of its 1798 or 1800 text, and the apparatus is plain that this is a thirty-six-poem selection rather than the complete contents.

reading.heading: First forms, two poets and places of encounter.
reading.note: Three routes consider what the earliest printings reveal, how the collaboration divided its forms and subjects, and the landscapes and meetings that carry the collection’s experiments.

work.heading: Starkfield reconstructed at twenty-four years’ distance.
work.note: The account below moves from the engineer’s arrival in Starkfield to Ethan’s life at twenty-eight, then to the novel’s 1911 publication, the French exercise Hiver behind it and the documented Lenox accident.

editorial.heading: The 1911 Scribner text and its Starkfield speech.
editorial.note: Wharton’s first book text is preserved down to its phonetic dialect, while notes and essays explain rural work and debt, winter transport, patent medicines, marriage and divorce.

reading.heading: Confinement, testimony and winter.
reading.note: Three routes weigh the material forces that close every exit, the partial testimony behind the engineer’s account, and the Starkfield winter that presses on each available choice.

work.heading: The Christmas books of 1843–48.
work.note: Dickens published five short books for the Christmas market in these years; the account below follows the four reprinted here, from Scrooge’s night of memory to Redlaw’s bargain to forget sorrow.

editorial.heading: How four Christmas books are framed as one volume.
editorial.note: Each book opens with a headnote on its first publication, and shared summaries, notes and context let the four plots be read against one another.

reading.heading: Four forms, poverty and memory.
reading.note: Three routes compare the shapes of Dickens’s short seasonal books, the judgement respectable opinion passes on poverty, and what the loss of memory does to sympathy.

work.heading: Seventeen documents, from private letters to the scaffold.
work.note: The sequence runs from letters to Henrietta Maria, the answers to the Petition of Right and the Declaration of Sports to Naseby, the High Court of Justice, the death warrant and the scaffold speech.

editorial.heading: Authorship and provenance stated for every document.
editorial.note: Each selection is identified as personal writing, formal drafting for the king, reported speech or doubtful attribution, with notes on people, law, Parliament and religion that keep the original wording.

reading.heading: The king’s hand, the conflict and the contest for memory.
reading.note: Three routes through the papers: separating what Charles wrote himself from texts composed in his name, reading the constitutional quarrel through its documents, and following the struggle over Eikon Basilike.

work.heading: Anne’s arrival and the first-edition text.
work.note: The novel begins with the mistake that sends Anne to the Cuthberts; the edition keeps Montgomery’s American spelling, contractions, dialect and punctuation as first printed in 1908.

editorial.heading: Montgomery’s language kept, recap and context separated.
editorial.note: Nothing is silently converted to later or British usage, and each chapter’s Story So Far summary stays distinct from its historical Context section.

reading.heading: An error, an island and a voice preserved.
reading.note: Three routes into the novel: how a mistaken arrival reshapes a family, how Avonlea sits in 1890s Prince Edward Island, and what the first-edition language keeps alive.

work.heading: Carroll’s final text and the manuscript behind it.
work.note: The 1865 book is given in Carroll’s last revised wording, with essays following its publication history, Oxford setting, Tenniel’s illustrations and the earlier Alice’s Adventures Under Ground.

editorial.heading: Support around Carroll’s language, not in place of it.
editorial.note: Chapter recaps and footnotes accompany the final revised text without replacing it, and manuscript comparisons show how Under Ground became the familiar printed book.

reading.heading: Recognition, revision and Tenniel’s pictures.
reading.note: Three routes into Wonderland: what Carroll’s first readers could identify, what changed between manuscript and book, and how the illustrations belong to its publication history.

work.heading: The Fifth of November across the nineteenth century.
work.note: Reprinted writing by Halliwell, Jerrold, Ainsworth, Paget, Chambers, Thiselton-Dyer and Hardy joins an 1888 newspaper survey and original chapters on the Plot, the Guy, fireworks, food and policing.

editorial.heading: Victorian sources marked off from the connecting chapters.
editorial.note: Notes and source statements say which pages reprint nineteenth-century writing and which are original chapters on law, manufacture, food and public order; a chronology and glossary run alongside.

reading.heading: Observance, regional custom and regulation.
reading.note: Three routes through the collection: how religious commemoration became public entertainment, how differently the night was kept across Britain, and how fireworks, parkin and policing tie spectacle to law and local economy.

work.heading: From the Cambridge papers to Judith Shakespeare.
work.note: The essay grew from papers read to women students at Newnham and Girton in October 1928; its argument moves through Oxbridge, Fernham, the British Museum and English literary history.

editorial.heading: Woolf’s text and notes, kept apart from the new apparatus.
editorial.note: Her spelling, punctuation and italics stand as she left them, and her own notes remain visibly distinct from the annotations that identify people, laws, money and institutions.

reading.heading: Money, invented figures and the literary record.
reading.note: Three routes through the essay: the material conditions of writing, the freedom Woolf gains by mixing fact with fiction, and the question of which women’s lives and works survive.

work.heading: A conspiracy told through many witnesses.
work.note: The account below follows the investigation, the narrators who assemble it and the revised text in which Collins settled the novel.

editorial.heading: The 1861 text and the history around it.
editorial.note: Concise footnotes restore what a Victorian reader would have recognised, and essays connect the narrative design to the law on which the plot depends.

reading.heading: Testimony, property and the power of institutions.
reading.note: Three routes through the novel, from the control of evidence to the marriage law and asylum practice that make the conspiracy work.

work.heading: Riverbank, Wild Wood and the roads of 1908.
work.note: The account below follows the four friends’ adventures and the Edwardian transport world that surrounds Toad’s machines.

editorial.heading: Grahame’s text intact, with notes around it.
editorial.note: Spelling and punctuation stay as first printed, while footnotes and essays explain the details that have grown unfamiliar since 1908.

reading.heading: Home, new machines and the rescue of Toad.
reading.note: Three routes through the book: belonging tested by wandering, old roads meeting motor cars, and the friendship that keeps correcting Toad.

work.heading: A diamond lost, and the witnesses who account for it.
work.note: The account below follows the investigation through its connected narrators, and the essays on serial publication, reception and the real history behind the famous diamond.

editorial.heading: Annotating without flattening the narrators.
editorial.note: Collins’s text is retained; the notes explain British India, Victorian policing and unfamiliar references while leaving each narrator’s voice distinct.

reading.heading: Testimony, empire and the making of detective fiction.
reading.note: Three routes follow witnesses whose accounts reveal themselves, the diamond’s contested passage from India, and the conventions of detection forming around the novel.

work.heading: Gregor Samsa’s transformation and the job he cannot miss.
work.note: The account below follows the Samsa household from the first missed train to the arrival of the lodgers, and records the writing of Die Verwandlung in twenty-one days of 1912.

editorial.heading: Johnston’s translation and the German behind it.
editorial.note: Ian Johnston’s public-domain translation stands, sixteen corrections aside, and the notes reach from the Prokurist’s authority and compulsory sickness insurance to the translation history of ungeheueres Ungeziefer.

reading.heading: Work, family money and a creature in translation.
reading.note: The routes below follow Gregor’s timetabled fear, the household economy that rearranges itself around him, and the English words that have tried to name his new body.

work.heading: The 1925 first edition and the summer of 1922.
work.note: The account below covers the novel’s publication on 10 April 1925, the first-edition text this edition follows, and the notes and essays that recover what Fitzgerald’s first readers recognised.

editorial.heading: Fitzgerald’s wording on one side, the 1920s on the other.
editorial.note: The first-edition spelling and punctuation stand unmodernised; chapter recaps, historical context and the essays on composition, reception and revival are kept clearly apart from the novel.

reading.heading: Place, money and the novel’s slow revival.
reading.note: Three routes follow the geography that organises social distance, the prices and brands that give 1922 material form, and the gap between first reception and later reputation.

work.heading: Six finished stories and four fragments from 1923.
work.note: The account below names the completed stories and the unfinished pieces, and follows the collection from Mansfield’s death to Murry’s assembly of the posthumous book.

editorial.heading: Mansfield’s fragments, identified rather than concealed.
editorial.note: The edition presents ten of the 1923 collection’s twenty-one items and says so; notes and chronology connect the stories to Wellington, domestic service and Mansfield’s final years.

reading.heading: Completion, class and the making of a posthumous book.
reading.note: Each route starts from the volume itself: the line between finished and unfinished work, the social divisions inside its closely observed rooms, and Murry’s part in bringing it to readers.

work.heading: Trotty Veck, the bells and the arguments of 1844.
work.note: The account below follows the story from Trotty’s post outside the church to the vision in the bell tower, and records its publication on 16 December 1844 as Dickens’s second Christmas book.

editorial.heading: Dickens’s dialect kept, the Poor Law explained.
editorial.note: What is Dickens’s and what is explanation is kept distinct, from the dialect on the page to the notes on the Poor Law and the 1840s reform debate.

reading.heading: Who defines poverty, and what future follows.
reading.note: Three routes into the book: the claims made over poor lives, the bells’ vision of where those claims lead, and the quarter chimes that give the story its shape.

work.heading: Twelve stories that became Halloween.
work.note: The account below names the writers and their works, from Irving to Lovecraft, none of them written for the holiday that later claimed them.

editorial.heading: Separating the stories from the holiday.
editorial.note: Publication histories and anachronism guides mark off what belongs to each story’s first printing from the associations October added later.

reading.heading: Twelve stories and the holiday that claimed them.
reading.note: Three routes follow the works before their seasonal adoption, the long line of American supernatural writing, and the making of an October canon.
